scope: Someone showed me a chart of average temperature against national income, and it looks like one of the tidiest things you will ever see in economics.
## The tidy story, and its correlation is real
![The tidy story, and its correlation is real](../charts/rf-1-the-tidy-story.png)
Average annual temperature against GDP per capita, every place with both, 197 countries and territories.
On log income the correlation is **minus 0.43**.
First, minus 0.43 accounts for about a fifth of the variation in log income, which leaves four fifths somewhere else.
On one common sample of 161 countries, temperature manages minus 0.47, absolute latitude does better at plus 0.61, and a plain Africa dummy does better still at minus 0.69.
Among the places Europeans would later colonise, temperature and population density in 1500 correlate at **plus 0.29** across 98 places.
The same thermometer correlates with income today at **minus 0.25** across 99, on a list that overlaps the first by 95.
It flips on a few cold places, though.
Drop Canada and the two correlations fall to plus 0.17 across 97 and minus 0.19 across 98, neither clear of chance.
Drop the four coldest former colonies, Canada, Chile, the United States and New Zealand, and they are plus 0.05 across 94 and minus 0.03 across 95.
The thermometer's flip is real in this sample, and fragile.
The reversal that does not depend on temperature at all comes next, and it is the one the argument rests on.
Across the 175 places with both measures, temperature against 1500 density is **minus 0.18**.
![Being densely settled in 1500 predicts poverty now, but only on one side of the split](../charts/rf-3-the-flip.png)
Across all 165 places with both, the correlation is **plus 0.04**.
Among 95 former colonies, being densely settled in 1500 correlates with income today at **minus 0.48**, which is firmly established.
Among the 70 not on that list it runs the other way at **plus 0.28**, which is weaker and only just clear of chance.
Fit them together with an interaction term and the slopes come out at plus 0.15 for places not on the list and minus 0.33 for the colonised, a gap with a t statistic of minus 5.3 across 165 places.
On their own 1995 income figures, recomputed from their file, the former-colony correlation is minus 0.58 across 91 countries; on 2023 income it is minus 0.48 across 95.
The urbanisation measure points the same way on much smaller samples, 43 former colonies and 45 other places: minus 0.42 among former colonies against plus 0.16 among the rest.
The gap between them is, with a t of minus 3.1.

**No explanation of the ranking between countries can rest only on an effect that was both constant over the period and the same whether or not Europeans arrived.** The test is on the effect, not the cause: the equator has not moved, but what it does to prosperity may have.
Heat acting directly and identically on human productivity is a casualty.
Among the 70 places not on AJR's list that are measurable in both eras, heat runs minus 0.15 then and minus 0.04 now, neither clear of chance.
Latitude sees it extremely well.
That second category is not a technicality; it contains an explanation in which a fixed tropical disease environment mattered enormously because of how it shaped European settlement.
A fourteen point slide, ranking 47th of 95.
Sudan, 92nd to 11th.

The first is that splitting on colonisation is not innocent: Europeans chose where to go partly on the basis of what was already there, and partly on things like latitude that correlate with income today, so the thing I am conditioning on sits downstream of one side of the comparison and upstream of the other.
That minus 0.74 measures the latitude part of it.
The chart that started me off is true and cannot mean what it looks like.

Among former colonies, places that were densely settled in 1500 tend to be poorer today, and an explanation whose effect never changed and never depended on whether Europeans arrived cannot account for that inversion.
It is just an easy thing to measure, and we have a habit of mistaking those for each other.
**Two transforms, both load-bearing.** Income is logged in every correlation except the raw-dollar figure the first chart also reports, minus 0.39 on 197.

So is population density in 1500, outside the untransformed check below: AJR's variable is already in logs, its own label reads "log population density, 1500", and the charts say so on their axes while an earlier version of these notes did not.
On untransformed density the former-colony correlation falls from minus 0.48 to minus 0.09 while the other falls to plus 0.17, so the two signs still point opposite ways.
But the interaction that the argument actually rests on falls from a t of minus 5.3 to minus 1.3, which is not distinguishable from zero.
**An assumption that is not a measurement.** The 1500 correlations use today's temperatures, because there is no 1991 to 2020 equivalent for 1500.

**Two of the bugs found in fact-checking, both fixed before publication.** The first: my de-duplication of the replication file kept the first row per country, and for Germany and Zimbabwe that row carries latitude but neither density nor income, so both were silently deleted from every correlation needing either.

**A bug found after publication.** A month after this post went up, a further fact-check found that Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson's files use pre-ISO codes for Romania, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the West Bank and Gaza, and that the two modern sources code Kosovo differently, so all four silently dropped out of every sample they belonged in.
Matching them moved the headline correlation and five other correlations by one in the second decimal and enlarged several samples slightly.

It also moved the urbanisation correlation for places not on AJR's list from plus 0.28 to plus 0.16, across 45, which weakens that check without reversing it: the gap between the groups still has a t of minus 3.1.
The falsification conditions still do not fire, and the interaction the argument rests on is unchanged at one decimal.
Both scripts now read through one loader, which asserts that every place with data finds its match.

Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson define it in several places in the paper, among them page 1243, the note to Table V and Appendix 2, as total population divided by arable land, excluding "primarily desert, inland water, and tundra".
Computing it showed the opposite, minus 0.18 across the 175 places with both measures.
**Which charts were chosen before the data and which after.** Chart one was specified before its ERA5 correlation was computed.
I had not written a condition for it.
**Samples.** The temperature and income chart uses all 197 entities with both, which includes territories such as Aruba, Greenland and Hong Kong SAR alongside sovereign states.
The historical comparisons use 95 former colonies and 70 places absent from AJR's ex-colony list with 1500 density and 2023 income.
Reclassifying nine awkward cases as colonies leaves the interaction at a t of minus 4.7, so the result does not depend on where they sit.

findings.claim: Someone showed me a chart of average temperature against national income, and it looks like one of the tidiest things you will ever see in economics.
findings.evidence: Nobody can check the anecdote, but it is the author's own testimony and makes no data claim. The data part holds up: with my own loader (scratchpad round2/DA/indep2.py), temperature against log 2023 GDP per capita gives r = -0.4336, n = 197, p about 2e-10. 'Looks like' describes an impression, and the post takes it apart three sentences later and again in sentence 5 (about a fifth of the variation). The excerpt was changed from 'is' to 'looks like' in round 1 (LG16), so the two now match.

findings.claim: ## The tidy story, and its correlation is real
findings.evidence: My own recomputation gives r = -0.4336, t = -6.72, n = 197, p about 2e-10, matching results.json tidy_story (r -0.43358, t -6.719). The heading claims only that the correlation is real, which is the narrowing LG11 asked for.

findings.claim: ![The tidy story, and its correlation is real](../charts/rf-1-the-tidy-story.png)
findings.evidence: I viewed charts/rf-1-the-tidy-story.png. Its title is 'The tidy story, and its correlation is real', matching the alt text and heading. The in-plot label reads 'r = -0.43 on log income   n = 197 countries and territories', and the footnote reads 'Every entity with both, 197 of them ... on raw dollars r is -0.39'. Both match my recomputation (raw-dollar r = -0.3862, n = 197).

findings.claim: Average annual temperature against GDP per capita, every place with both, 197 countries and territories.
findings.evidence: I checked this independently. wb_gdp_2023.json has 241 rows with a value. 44 of them have no CCKP temperature, and every one of those 44 is a World Bank aggregate (AFE ... WLD, plus the empty-code 'Upper middle income' row). That leaves 197 entities with both, and no real economy with a 2023 GDP lacks an ERA5 temperature once KSV is mapped to XKX. The 49 CCKP places without GDP (CUB, VEN, ERI, TWN, ...) have no World Bank 2023 value, so 'every place with both' is exhaustive. findings.claim: On log income the correlation is minus 0.43.
findings.evidence: My recomputation gives r = -0.4336 (n = 197), which rounds to -0.43, matching results.json tidy_story.r = -0.43358. Before the fix it was -0.4352 (rounded -0.44, per results-old.json). The new value is the one printed.

findings.claim: First, minus 0.43 accounts for about a fifth of the variation in log income, which leaves four fifths somewhere else.
findings.evidence: r^2 = 0.18799, so rest_share = 0.81201 (results.json tidy_story.r2_share and rest_share, and my own recomputation gives 0.1880). 0.188 is 'about a fifth' and 0.812 is 'four fifths'. With the rounded figure, 0.43^2 = 0.185, so the wording fits either way.

findings.claim: On one common sample of 161 countries, temperature manages minus 0.47, absolute latitude does better at plus 0.61, and a plain Africa dummy does better still at minus 0.69.
findings.evidence: I independently dropped every row missing tas, log 2023 GDP, lat_abst or africa and got n = 161. The three correlations are temperature -0.4689, latitude +0.6092 and Africa -0.6885, which round to -0.47, +0.61 and -0.69. The magnitudes are ordered 0.47 < 0.61 < 0.69, so 'better' and 'better still' still hold after each value moved by 0.01 from -0.46/+0.60/-0.68. Minor: the 161 includes one territory (HKG), so 'countries' is a slight approximation, much smaller than the 5 and 10 territories in the 165 and 175 samples that LG21 renamed 'places'.

findings.claim: Among the places Europeans would later colonise, temperature and population density in 1500 correlate at plus 0.29 across 98 places.
findings.evidence: In my recomputation, among ex2col==1 rows the correlation is +0.2945, n = 98, p = 0.0033, matching heat_reversal.former_colonies.vs_density_1500 (r 0.29445, n 98). The count rose from 97 when ZAR was mapped to COD. Pedantic note: the 98 include Cape Verde, the Dominican Republic and Haiti, where Portuguese or Spanish settlement began before 1500, so 'would later' is approximate for those three. The wording is unchanged by round 1 and does not affect the figure.

findings.claim: The same thermometer correlates with income today at minus 0.25 across 99, on a list that overlaps the first by 95.
findings.evidence: In my recomputation, former colonies give temperature against log 2023 GDP r = -0.2503, n = 99, p = 0.012. The density list (98) and the income list (99) share 95 places. Only in density: CUB, ERI, VEN. Only in income: BTN, DJI, FJI, MUS. This matches heat_reversal_overlap (n 95).

findings.claim: It flips on a few cold places, though.
findings.evidence: Removing Canada alone takes both correlations below conventional significance: +0.1692 (p = 0.098, n = 97) and -0.1864 (p = 0.066, n = 98). Removing CAN, CHL, USA and NZL leaves +0.055 and -0.035. A few cold places carry the flip.

findings.claim: Drop Canada and the two correlations fall to plus 0.17 across 97 and minus 0.19 across 98, neither clear of chance.
findings.evidence: My own recomputation gives +0.1692, n = 97, p = 0.0975 and -0.1864, n = 98, p = 0.0661. Both magnitudes fall (0.29 to 0.17, 0.25 to 0.19), and both p-values are above the 5% level the post uses elsewhere ('only just clear of chance' at p = 0.019). This matches heat_reversal_robustness.without_canada.

findings.claim: Drop the four coldest former colonies, Canada, Chile, the United States and New Zealand, and they are plus 0.05 across 94 and minus 0.03 across 95.
findings.evidence: I re-derived this myself (scratchpad/round2/draftA-adj/da11.py, which runs build_analysis.load()). The numbers are right. Dropping CAN, CHL, USA and NZL gives r = +0.0547 with n = 94 against 1500 density and r = -0.0347 with n = 95 against 2023 income. These match results.json heat_reversal_robustness.without_coldest. The label is false, though. AJR's raw files code BTN as ex2col = 1.0 with lpd1500s NaN (data/ajr_t5/maketable5.dta and data/ajr_t3/maketable3.dta). Its ERA5 temperature is 9.59 C and it has lgdp2023 = 9.59. Ranked by temperature, the former colonies with temperature data run CAN -3.72, CHL 8.96, BTN 9.59, USA 9.67, NZL 10.24. So the four coldest former colonies are CAN, CHL, BTN and USA, not the four the sentence names. BTN is in the n = 99 income sample (results.json heat_reversal_overlap.only_income = [BTN, DJI, FJI, MUS]). It stays in the n = 95 sample after the drop, so the income figure the sentence reports still contains a former colony colder than two of the four dropped. Bhutan is also plotted in chart 2's right panel. Dropping the true four (CAN, CHL, BTN, USA) gives +0.093 with n = 95 and -0.079 with n = 95. The code picks its four only among colonies with 1500 density (build_analysis.py:232, col_t.dropna(subset=['lpd1500s']).nsmallest(4,'tas')). The gate.toml:153 licence states that qualifier, but the prose at src.md:53 drops it. The same unqualified label appears in the chart 2 footnote (make_charts.py:163-164, 'without the {n_coldest} coldest former colonies') and in live MDX lines 51 and 69. The post itself says it uses AJR's own ex-colony classification, so Bhutan counts as a former colony by the post's definition. The refuter did not over-reach.

findings.claim: Across the 175 places with both measures, temperature against 1500 density is minus 0.18.
findings.evidence: AJR has 177 rows with lpd1500s. Only ANT and YUG lack an ERA5 temperature (defunct, no modern counterpart), so 175 is every place with both. This makes the 'with both measures' framing true where round 1 FX1 found it false at 173. My recomputation gives r = -0.1822, p = 0.016, which rounds to -0.18. findings.claim: ![Being densely settled in 1500 predicts poverty now, but only on one side of the split](../charts/rf-3-the-flip.png)
findings.evidence: I viewed rf-3-the-flip.png. The suptitle matches the alt text exactly. The panels show r = -0.48, n = 95 (colonised) and r = +0.28, n = 70 (not on AJR's list), and the footnote gives pooled +0.04 (n = 165), 1995 -0.58 and 2023 -0.48. All match my recomputation. 'Predicts poverty only on one side' holds: the negative association appears only among former colonies, and the other group's sign is positive.

CUB, ERI, PYF, SYR, VEN, VIR and YEM are present with a null value. So 165 is exhaustive. My recomputation gives r = +0.0425, p = 0.59, which rounds to +0.04. No row with density has a null ex2col, so the 165 equal the 95 + 70 split.

findings.claim: Among 95 former colonies, being densely settled in 1500 correlates with income today at minus 0.48, which is firmly established.
findings.evidence: My recomputation gives r = -0.4794, n = 95, p about 8e-7, t = -5.27. 'Firmly established' fits. The Spearman correlation, which does not change under the log transform, is -0.400 with p = 5.8e-5, so the monotone association does not depend on logging density. The value moved from -0.49 (n 94) to -0.48 (n 95), and the wording still fits.

findings.claim: Among the 70 not on that list it runs the other way at plus 0.28, which is weaker and only just clear of chance.
findings.evidence: My recomputation gives r = +0.2806, n = 70, t = 2.41, p = 0.0186, essentially unchanged from +0.2800 on 69. 'Weaker' (0.28 against 0.48) holds. 'Only just clear of chance' is fair, if conservative: it clears the 5% level but not the 1% level. If anything it understates the evidence, since Spearman is +0.39 with p = 0.0008, so it does not overstate the thesis.

findings.claim: Fit them together with an interaction term and the slopes come out at plus 0.15 for places not on the list and minus 0.33 for the colonised, a gap with a t statistic of minus 5.3 across 165 places.
findings.evidence: I fitted my own numpy OLS of lg ~ lpd1500s + ex2col + lpd1500s*ex2col on n = 165. Slopes: +0.1480 for not on the list and -0.3338 for colonised. Interaction t = -5.292, p = 3.9e-7, and with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) errors t = -5.78. This matches results.json interaction (t -5.2915, n 165). The value moved from -5.33 to -5.29 and still rounds to -5.3.

findings.claim: On their own 1995 income figures, recomputed from their file, the former-colony correlation is minus 0.58 across 91 countries; on 2023 income it is minus 0.48 across 95.
findings.evidence: My recomputation gives -0.5842 on n = 91 for logpgp95 among ex2col==1, and -0.4794 on n = 95 for log 2023 GDP. Both match results.json flip['density_1500|income_1995|former_colonies'] and ['density_1500|income_2023|former_colonies']. The 1995 figure is unchanged by the code fixes, since the legacy-code places lack 1995 values in the colony sample.

findings.claim: The urbanisation measure points the same way on much smaller samples, 43 former colonies and 45 other places: minus 0.42 among former colonies against plus 0.16 among the rest.
findings.evidence: My recomputation gives -0.4239 on n = 43 (p = 0.005) and +0.1646 on n = 45 (p = 0.28), matching results.json. The signs match the density pattern, so 'points the same way' holds. 'Much smaller' holds: 88 against 165 overall, and 43 against 95 for colonies. The next sentence ('The second of those is not significant on its own') correctly fits the new value: the old +0.28 had p of about 0.07, and the new +0.16 has p = 0.28, which is more clearly not significant.

findings.claim: The gap between them is, with a t of minus 3.1.
findings.evidence: My own interaction OLS of lg on sjb1500*ex2col gives n = 88, t = -3.124, p = 0.0025 (84 degrees of freedom), and HC1 robust t = -3.60. That is significant, so 'The gap between them is [significant]' holds after the move from -3.6 to -3.1. Matches interaction_urbanisation.t = -3.1238.

findings.claim: No explanation of the ranking between countries can rest only on an effect that was both constant over the period and the same whether or not Europeans arrived. The test is on the effect, not the cause: the equator has not moved, but what it does to prosperity may have.
findings.evidence: Suppose the only driver were an effect identical in 1500 and today, and identical in both groups. Then 1500 density and today's income would move together in the same direction in both groups. The data show opposite signs (-0.48 and +0.28) and a significant gap (interaction t = -5.29, p = 3.9e-7). 'Rest only on' (the LG4 narrowing) leaves room for explanations that combine a constant effect with European selection. That selection channel is disclosed in the method notes ('splitting on colonisation is not innocent'). The claim is a logical one and is supported by the interaction test.

findings.claim: Heat acting directly and identically on human productivity is a casualty.
findings.evidence: This follows from the filter in sentence 23. A heat effect that is constant over time and the same in both groups is a special case of the excluded class, and the density reversal it cannot produce does not involve temperature (interaction t = -5.29). Round 1 LG2 removed the overreaching 'clearest casualty ... did the opposite' clause, and the bare 'a casualty' no longer leans on the fragile heat flip.

findings.claim: Among the 70 places not on AJR's list that are measurable in both eras, heat runs minus 0.15 then and minus 0.04 now, neither clear of chance.
findings.evidence: I computed this on ex2col==0 rows with tas, lpd1500s and log 2023 GDP all present: n = 70. Temperature against 1500 density gives -0.1546 (p = 0.20), and against income -0.0423 (p = 0.73). Both match never_colonised_common_sample. The common-sample restriction is stated ('measurable in both eras'). Context: on all 87 such places with income the 'now' figure is -0.29, but the 17 dropped are mostly small islands with no 1500 density (BRN, CYP, FRO, FSM, GRL, KIR, MAC, MDV, MHL, PLW, PSE, SLB, STP, SYC, TON, VUT, WSM), so a matched comparison is the right one.

findings.claim: Latitude sees it extremely well.
findings.evidence: My recomputation of absolute latitude against ex2col gives r = -0.7416, n = 167. The AUC of latitude for separating colonised from not is 0.927, which supports 'extremely well'. The next sentence's 'tighter than any relationship elsewhere in this post' holds: the next largest magnitude is Africa at -0.69.

findings.claim: Draft :53 (MDX :69): 'The reversal that does not depend on temperature at all comes next, and it is the one the argument rests on.' This shifts the argument's weight from the heat flip to the density reversal.
findings.evidence: I recomputed with build_analysis.load() (scratch round2/argument/probe2.py). The density reversal does not share the heat flip's fragility. findings.claim: The filter's logical step. Draft :91-96 (MDX :112-114): 'If something pressed equally on prosperity in 1500 and today, and pressed equally on places Europeans reached and places they did not, it cannot produce a ranking that inverted in one group and did not in the other.' With :103-104: 'It is disqualified only if its effect also held steady across the five centuries.'
findings.evidence: The step is stated as a logical impossibility, and it fails under selection into the groups. In sim_ar7.py, latitude raises 1500 density and income by fixed amounts that are the same in both eras and both groups, and density has no effect of its own. Selection is 'colonised if tropical, or sparse anywhere'. That gives pooled +0.184, colonised -0.085 and not colonised +0.044: opposite within-group signs with no effect changing. The real data carry the signature (ar567.py). Latitude against log 1500 density is +0.256 pooled (n=161, p=0.001), -0.222 within colonies (n=97, p=0.029) and +0.151 within the rest (n=64). Latitude against colonisation is -0.742 (n=167), which is the very fact the :100-104 passage cites. Empirically the route is small. Adding latitude with a shared coefficient leaves the interaction at -0.457, t=-5.02 (n=156), and adding tas leaves t=-5.01 (n=165). The post reports neither test. The post's selection caveat comes later (:147-151), and the filter does not carry it.

findings.claim: Close, draft :165-167 (MDX :187-189): 'Among former colonies, places that were densely settled in 1500 tend to be poorer today, and an explanation whose effect never changed and never depended on whether Europeans arrived cannot account for that inversion.' Does it follow from the filter?
findings.evidence: It follows from the narrowed filter. An effect that never changed pushes the 1500 and 2023 rankings the same way, so it cannot supply a sign inversion. The 'never depended' clause only narrows the class further. The empirical premise is robust: r=-0.479 (n=95). Spearman is -0.400 (p=6e-5), which is invariant to the log transform, so 'tend to be poorer' does not depend on the logging that the method notes say the t-test needs. It holds without the neo-Europes (-0.379, p=0.0002). For the two constant candidates the post names, 'cannot account' is borne out: the interaction stays at t=-5.02 with a latitude control and t=-5.01 with a temperature control. As a general proposition it inherits AR7's selection caveat.

findings.claim: [data/README.md] temp1 through temp5 are withdrawn. They are documented (Appendix 2, sourced to Parker 1997) but they fail a sanity check as country annual means: the United States reads 27 degrees and Greenland 26, and they correlate at only 0.58 with ERA5 over 203 matched countries.
findings.evidence: temp1_sanity() reads only temp1 (build_analysis.py:136). USA 27, GRL 26 and r 0.5811 on n_matched 203 are all temp1 (results.json withdrawn_temp1_sanity_check). Appendix 2 (sources/ajr2002.txt:2407-2410) defines the five as average temperature, minimum and maximum monthly high, and minimum and maximum monthly low, so temp2 to temp5 are not annual means by definition. I recomputed each against ERA5 on the same 203 matched rows: temp2 r 0.567, temp3 0.031, temp4 0.674, temp5 0.365. Their USA values are 32, 37, 15 and 21. So 'they fail a sanity check as country annual means ... they correlate at only 0.58' gives one variable's figures to all five. The sentence is in scope because n_matched moved from 200 (results-old.json) to 203 under the code fix. Of the 203 matched codes, about 20 are territories or non-sovereign (ABW, ASM, BMU, CYM, FRO, GLP, GRL, GUF, GUM, HKG, MAC, MNP, MTQ, MYT, NCL, PRI, PYF, REU, VIR, plus PSE/TWN), including the Greenland the sentence itself names, so 'countries' is loose.

findings.claim: The first is that splitting on colonisation is not innocent: Europeans chose where to go ... partly on things like latitude that correlate with income today, so the thing I am conditioning on sits downstream of one side of the comparison and upstream of the other.
findings.evidence: Latitude does correlate with income today: rivals_common_sample.lat_abst r=+0.609, n=161, t=9.7. The split is tied to latitude: colonisation_vs_latitude r=-0.742, n=167. Round 1's narrowing ('correlate with' instead of 'shape', LG14) is accurate. Settlement responding to local conditions is AJR's own account (ajr2002.txt:1732-1735). The sentence is a stated caveat rather than a causal claim, and nothing in it is false as written.

findings.claim: That minus 0.74 measures the latitude part of it.
findings.evidence: I re-derived this with build_analysis.load(). The figure is right: colonisation_vs_latitude r = -0.7416 on n = 167. What the sentence says the figure measures is not. Of the 66 ex2col = 0 places that have lat_abst, 37 are European states (AUT, BEL, ..., GBR, ..., ROU, RUS, ..., YUG). No European power chose to colonise any of them. Mean lat_abst is 0.464 for the never-colonised places and 0.178 for the colonies. With those 37 removed, r(lat_abst, ex2col) = -0.5246 on 130. Src:148-150 sets the number against 'Europeans chose where to go ... partly on things like latitude' and then calls -0.74 'the latitude part of it', so a reader takes it as the size of a choice. Much of the -0.74 comes from the colonisers' own high latitude, which is not a choice. Two things are true as written: -0.74 is how tightly the conditioning split tracks latitude, and that is the quantity that matters for the conditioning caveat. So the number can stay, but the attribution has to narrow. Round 1 (LG12) put in 'the latitude part of it' as a narrowing and never tested the composition of the comparison group.
findings.fix: Draft src:150 and live MDX:172: replace 'That {{colonisation_vs_latitude.r:signed2}} measures the latitude part of it.' with 'That {{colonisation_vs_latitude.r:signed2}} measures how closely the split tracks latitude.' Deleting the sentence would also work.

findings.claim: The chart that started me off is true and cannot mean what it looks like.

The post's own figures rule that reading out. tidy_story.r2_share is 0.188, so four fifths of the variation lies elsewhere. Within 24-28 C, income runs from $1,133 to $130,297 (spread_24_28c). A constant heat effect cannot produce the density reversal (interaction.t -5.29). 'True' refers to the chart, meaning the correlation is real (r -0.434, t -6.7); it is not the causal reading that round 1 narrowed in the heading. With the 'because' clause deleted, the support now comes from the next sentence, which holds.

findings.claim: Among former colonies, places that were densely settled in 1500 tend to be poorer today, and an explanation whose effect never changed and never depended on whether Europeans arrived cannot account for that inversion.
findings.evidence: results.json flip density_1500|income_2023|former_colonies r=-0.479, n=95, t=-5.27, so 'tend to be poorer' holds. The interaction gap has t=-5.29 on 165. The second clause is a valid logical statement: an effect that is constant over time cannot reorder a ranking, so the extra condition only narrows it. The density-as-prosperity assumption behind 'inversion' is disclosed at draft:153-159.

findings.claim: It is just an easy thing to measure, and we have a habit of mistaking those for each other.
findings.evidence: Low severity. The word 'just' was already there: before round 1 the line read 'It is just the easiest thing to measure' (git diff of the live MDX against 8cb1520). Round 1's CB22 changed only 'the easiest' to 'an easy', so the sentence is replacement prose. 'An easy thing to measure' is true. 'Just' (merely) adds the implicature that the thermometer is nothing more than a convenient variable. The post concedes the opposite in three places. Src:137 says 'It does not show that temperature is irrelevant to income'. Src:141-142 calls Dell et al. (2012) 'evidence of a real effect of heat on output'. Src:169, the sentence right before, says the thermometer 'cannot be the whole of it', which implies it is part of it. The closing line takes back what the post concedes.
findings.fix: Draft src:170 and live MDX:192: delete 'just ', leaving 'It is an easy thing to measure, and we have a habit of mistaking those for each other.'

findings.claim: An assumption that is not a measurement. The 1500 correlations use today's temperatures, because there is no 1991 to 2020 equivalent for 1500.
findings.evidence: Every temperature in the 1500 correlations is `tas`, the CCKP ERA5 1991-2020 annual climatology (build_analysis.py:70-71, 176-177, 224-227, 245-248). ERA5 is an observation-based reanalysis with no counterpart for 1500; only proxy reconstructions exist, which are not equivalent. The new header ('An assumption', round 1's AL22 change) is a correct singular.

findings.claim: Two of the bugs found in fact-checking, both fixed before publication. findings.claim: A month after this post went up, a further fact-check found that Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson's files use pre-ISO codes for Romania, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the West Bank and Gaza, and that the two modern sources code Kosovo differently, so all four silently dropped out of every sample they belonged in.
findings.evidence: (1) 'Pre-ISO' is wrong. ROM and ZAR were ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 codes, and Wikipedia's 'ISO 3166-1 alpha-3' page (fetched today) lists both as transitional reservations: ROM from February 2002 (changed to ROU) and ZAR from July 1997. WBG appears nowhere on that page. It was never an ISO code. (2) 'Every sample they belonged in' is false. I emulated the pre-fix loader with AJR_CODE_FIXES and TAS_CODE_FIXES cleared. ROM and ZAR were still in lpd1500s x logpgp95 (n = 156) and lat_abst x ex2col (n = 167), and ROM was in sjb1500 x logpgp95 (n = 84). That matches results-old.json, where flip density_1500|income_1995 (r = 0.0517 on 156; -0.5842 on 91) and colonisation_vs_latitude (-0.7416 on 167) equal today's values. The refuter's proposed wording is also false. The World Bank and the CCKP both use ROU, COD and PSE, so Romania, the DR Congo and Palestine were inside the pre-fix tidy-story sample of temperature x 2023 income (n = 196). Only XKX was missing, because the CCKP codes Kosovo as KSV. So the three AJR places did not drop out of 'every sample that needed a temperature or 2023 income'. They dropped out only where AJR's codes had to be matched to a modern source, and Kosovo dropped out only where the two modern sources had to be matched to each other. The rest of the claim is correct: the post went live on 2026-09-07 (8cb1520), the bug was found on 2026-10-09, and Kosovo is KSV in data/cckp_tas.json and XKX in the World Bank file.
